title: The "12 months vs 24 months" banking conflict is not a conflict
where_published: pages/flagged.html (F1), data/flagged.csv (F1), pages/allowed-increases.html, pages/sources.html, dashboard/flagged.html and data/flagged.json (FL-03), dashboard/executive-summary.html, EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY.md, internal/notes.md, COORDINATION.md
published_statement: "sf.gov says a skipped increase banks only after 24 months; the ordinance says otherwise" and "the Rent Board's own worked examples bank an increase after 12 months"
official_finding: Rule 4.12(a) requires a full 12 months from the date each increase could first be imposed; the banked-increases page says at least 24 full months without any increase. The first skipped increase only becomes available 12 months after the last increase or lease start, so for it the two statements are the same test (12 + 12 = 24). The Ordinance (Sec. 37.3(a)(2)) states no waiting period; the period sits in the Rules. A model of Rule 4.12(a) reproduces all four of the Rent Board's own worked examples, including the one where a 1.4% increase is lost after 35 months without an increase, which a loose reading of the 24-month sentence would wrongly bank.
requested_action: Reword F1 / FL-03 from "conflict" to "resolved on the text; optional confirmation with the Rent Board counselor". State the result: Unit 1's 1.4% (available 2026-02-01) banks only if the increase takes effect on or after 2027-02-01; an earlier effective date forfeits it. The 1.6%-only option remains lawful for an earlier date.

title: Penal Code 396 is cited at the wrong subdivision and without its extension rule
published_statement: "during a declared emergency, Penal Code 396(b) makes it unlawful to raise housing costs more than 10% ... for 30 days after the declaration"
official_finding: The rent-specific rule is subdivision (e): 30 days "or any period the proclamation or declaration is extended by the applicable authority", and "This subdivision does not authorize a landlord to charge a price greater than the amount authorized by a local rent control ordinance." Subdivision (g) allows extensions of up to 30 days each. Subdivision (j)(2) ties "local emergency" to disaster-type emergencies, so whether the 2026 "rent emergency" qualifies is not established.
requested_action: Cite subdivision (e) and add "or any extension"; add one flagged item: coverage by the 2026 rent emergency and any extension are unverified (official proclamation not retrieved); get counsel's view before serving an increase above 10%.

title: Sec. 37.10B(a)(5) is described more broadly than its text
where_published: dashboard/market.html, build.py (line 519 and 844), data/questions.json, data/facts.json, data/sources.json
published_statement: "Sec. 37.10B(a)(5) treats a rent increase 'substantially in excess of market rates for comparable units' as evidence of bad faith where a tenant believes an increase is aimed at getting them out"
official_finding: The listed bad-faith evidence is attached to one example: a rent increase on a unit exempt from rent limits, imposed with intent to defraud, intimidate or coerce the tenant into vacating in circumvention of the just-cause rules. It does not turn every large lawful increase on a controlled unit into evidence of bad faith, and it turns on the landlord's intent, not on what the tenant believes. The practical exposure for a 13.1% banked increase is better described by: nonconforming notice (null and void), no license on the effective date, retaliation timing (Civil Code 1942.5), discrimination (Sec. 37.10B(a)(9)), and the pending cap.
